entry.title: A solver, an assistant, and a flag that says simulated

link.title: A solver, an assistant, and a flag that says simulated

entry.content:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how an AI assistant gets tools: a server describes what it can do, and the assistant calls it. Ansys ships MCP servers for Fluent, Mechanical, MAPDL, AEDT, CFX and Lumerical. It does not ship one for Rocky, its discrete element method (DEM) solver. DEM is how granular material gets simulated: bulk solids, powders and, if you work on railways, ballast.

Rocky does have a Python client, ansys-rocky-core. But a client is an API, not a tool an assistant can pick up. Without a server, someone writes the PyRocky boilerplate by hand every time. So I wrote ansys-rocky-mcp. It is an independent project under MIT, built on ansys-common-mcp so it follows the same pattern as the PyAnsys servers.

What it can do

There are 25 tools. They open and save projects, import walls, and define particles, inlets, outlets, the domain and solver settings. They apply motion, start a run and wait for it. Then they read curves, grid-function statistics and selections. One more tool runs arbitrary Python in a persistent session, for everything the other 25 do not cover.

The part I care about

There are two backends. pyrocky drives a real, licensed Rocky. mock is an in-memory stand-in. It tracks the whole study setup and returns time series that are physically consistent and completely made up. The mock is useful: you can try the server, write a workflow, and test a client with no licence at all.

It is also dangerous, for the same reason. An assistant that quietly falls back to the mock produces a clean mass-flow curve that no solver ever computed. It looks like a result. It will be pasted into a slide as a result.

So three rules:

  1. Every response carries backend and simulated fields. Whatever the assistant sees, it also sees where the numbers came from.
  2. The server tells the assistant to say so. If simulated is true, the instructions require it to tell the user that the numbers did not come from Ansys Rocky.
  3. The default never substitutes. auto uses the real Rocky when it is installed. When it is not, it fails with an error that says what to install. It never switches to mock numbers on its own.

This is the same rule this blog keeps applying. Pseudo-PFLOW does not show an unpublished fit. BKK/FLOW leaves flood depth empty rather than map a noise field. A tool that hands an assistant numbers should be at least as honest about where they came from as I try to be.

Status

The full workflow has been tested end to end over a real MCP stdio connection, with 42 automated tests. It runs over stdio or HTTP and needs Python 3.12 or newer. The real backend needs Rocky 2024 R2 or newer. Setup for Claude, Codex, Cursor, MiniMax and Kimi is in the repository.
entry.summary: An MCP server for Ansys Rocky. 25 tools, two backends, and why every response says whether its numbers came from the solver.

entry.title: A station a day
entry.content:
Eki-dle is a side project. It is also the cheapest way I know to learn a rail network: guess a station, get a distance and a direction, guess again. Play it at wattwong103.github.io/Eki-dle. The code is on GitHub.

There are six modes. Station gives you six tries, with distance, compass direction, prefecture, region and shared-line hints. Kana is Wordle for five-kana station names. Line asks for the day’s railway line. Map shows a fixed, unlabelled map. Code gives station numbering codes, one more per miss. Diagram shows a schematic of the nearby stops with no names. Puzzles change at midnight Japan time, with separate dailies by region, city, operator, Shinkansen or JR.

The hints are a geography lesson

Station mode’s hints are a small model of how people actually place a station. Same prefecture or neighbouring prefecture. A shared line, or at least the same operator. Kilometres and a bearing. After a few rounds the useful move is to stop guessing famous names and think in corridors: which way the bearing points, and which operator would explain that yellow square.

Choosing the answers is a design decision

There are about 9,000 operating stations, and every one is a valid guess. Only about 1,100 can be a daily answer: transfer stations, Shinkansen stops and a handful of famous terminals. A daily puzzle has to be fair to someone who has never left Tokyo. A one-platform halt in rural Hokkaido is a fine practice round and a miserable daily.

Line mode uses the same logic. About 490 lines have enough stations to be guessable. A city’s line pool only includes lines with at least three stops in that city. If an area has no possible answers for a mode, the game says so instead of quietly using all of Japan.

The data comes from station_database, CC BY 4.0. The maps are OpenFreeMap tiles drawn with Leaflet and MapLibre.

Two rules it does not break

Never frame the map on the answer. If the opening view is centred on the hidden station, the map has already told you. The opening bounds always use the whole selected area, never the answer. Tests guard this, along with the next rule.

Never let a label flash. Map mode removes labels and place icons before drawing. When you switch modes or languages, the old frame stays covered until the new style has finished rendering. Otherwise a station name can show for one frame, which is exactly long enough to spoil the puzzle.

Small enough to load on a train

The map engine is about 1.06 MB before compression, so it now loads only when a map is on screen. That cut the JavaScript loaded at startup from about 237 kB to 82 kB. The build now fails if startup JavaScript goes over 110 kB. Without a connection or WebGL you still get a bundled outline of Japan and an honest error message, not a blank page.

Version 1.0 went out on 14 September with 101 automated tests. If it teaches you one new transfer station, it has done its job.
entry.summary: Eki-dle, a daily puzzle on Japan's 9,000 stations, and two rules it does not break. Never frame the map on the answer. Never let a label flash.

entry.title: Shibuya has no denominator
entry.content:
In a four-step model a station is a node. In Shibuya it is eight levels, from the Ginza Line on 3F to platforms five floors underground, run by several operators. Which exit you take decides which street gets the crowd. I wanted to see that, so I built the Shibuya Station Atlas: a rotatable 3D model and a 2D floor plan that share the same geometry and selection. It is live at wattwong103.github.io/transit-layout.

Version 1.0.0 covers the eight levels, eight surrounding building envelopes and 20 selected exits. Every shape in it is labelled schematic. This post is about why.

The prototype looked finished

The first version drew nicely. Then I audited it. The coordinates were authored on a 1400 × 900 drawing with no geographic reference, no scale and no measured elevations. Comments like “OSM/Google” sat next to shapes, which is not provenance anyone can reproduce. Floor heights were display indices, not metres. Because 1F was 1 and B1 was −1, that one gap was drawn twice as tall as every other.

The walking graph checked out: 86 nodes, 113 edges, 44 regions, 8 floors, no duplicate IDs, fully connected. That proves the data agrees with itself, and nothing more. The step-free subgraph split into four disconnected pieces. That does not show Shibuya has no step-free route between those floors. It shows the dataset has none.

Public sources, and their dates

The best public source is MLIT’s PLATEAU model of the underground passages by the west exit. I downloaded it and opened the archive: 59 tiles, 343 feature IDs, four room IDs, one building. It is a real start for one small area, not the station, and its geometry still has to be decoded and checked.

The dates disagree. The PLATEAU catalogue gives a reference date of December 2024. The operator floor guides I compared against are from 2026, and Shibuya has kept changing in between. The atlas keeps those conflicts visible instead of choosing one quietly.

No denominator

The audit has one line I keep coming back to: the denominator is unknown. I have not found a complete list of Shibuya’s exits, connections and public passages across all the operators and buildings. Without one, “covers 80% of exits” is a number I would be making up. So the atlas claims none. It shows 20 selected exits, each link carries its source and date, and a dashed line means “an exit toward a destination”, not a route you can walk.

What it does not map is just as explicit: measured geometry, building interiors, step-free routes and current closures.

What measured would take

Metric polygons with their original coordinate transforms. Level IDs per facility, with unknown elevations allowed. Checkpoints held out of the alignment so the error can actually be measured. Dated records of closures and access. And someone standing at the exits, checking sign text and which landings a lift actually serves.

That is a lot of work for one station. It is also the honest price of saying “here is how you get from the Hanzomon platform to the street”. Until it is paid, the atlas is a way to understand the station’s shape, not a way to navigate it.
entry.summary: Building a 3D atlas of an eight-level station from public sources, and why every shape in it is still labelled schematic.

entry.title: A flood map that is really a noise field

link.title: A flood map that is really a noise field

entry.content:
BKK/FLOW asks a Tokyo question about Bangkok. PFLOW describes a city as people, their activities, their trips and their trajectories. What happens to that picture when the water comes up? The code is on GitHub, and everything in it is built from open data: OpenStreetMap, WorldPop and JRC Global Surface Water.

The pilot is Khlong San, on the Thonburi bank of the Chao Phraya: 5.96 km², 115,959 modelled residents, and a walk network of 7,514 directed edges. The current demonstration release went out on 11 October.

Not better than Pseudo-PFLOW

The comparison is written down in the repository, headline first. Pseudo-PFLOW covers all 1,724 municipalities in Japan, with census-derived person attributes and calibrated behaviour. It reports an R² of 0.81 against mobile-phone location data at 1 km. BKK/FLOW has modelled age per cell and nothing calibrated. Sex is a scenario assumption.

What it does have is a hazard dimension and a paper trail: a licence-aware source registry, immutable runs with manifests, and an API that only reads those runs. That is a real difference. It is not a substitute, and pretending otherwise is the quickest way to lose a reviewer.

One terrain tile

The plan said: take a digital elevation model, set a water surface, subtract, and get depth. The only terrain reachable from my setup was an SRTM-family tile service at about 19 m per pixel. For the tile over central Bangkok, which includes all of Khlong San, the mean elevation was 7.76 m. The real ground there is 1–2 m above sea level.

A transect across the Chao Phraya, sampled every 150 m, read like this:

9  8  9  4  4  10  7  9  9  7  5  5  10  9  7  10  9  3  10  11  10  8  13  15 ...

There is no river in it. The lowest reading is about 3 m, where the riverbed should be below sea level.

Bangkok’s flood-relevant terrain spans about 0–2 m. This data carries ±5–10 m of error over that same range. Depth is water surface minus terrain, so every depth it produced would be mostly noise, and the flooded area would trace the error pattern instead of the hydrology. Nudge the assumed water level and you get changes that look plausible and mean nothing.

A map that looks like a flood map and is really a noise field is worse than no map, because people will read it as a flood map. So city-scale flood depth and evacuation outcomes are null in BKK/FLOW, and each null carries its reason. The gap is on the record. Nobody missed it.

What it can say

JRC annual surface water is observed, not modelled, so the city run uses it. The question is narrow: when road edges that touch water close, what share of the residents near water can still reach the network? Across 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2020 the answer is about 95.5–97.8%, depending on the year and how many wet edges close. That is connectivity, not evacuation success. Routing ignores one-way streets, and foot access is an assumption.

There are also 1,034 candidate destinations tagged as shelters, schools, hospitals and community buildings. None is verified. A tag is not capacity, and it is not a promise of a dry route.

That city run has since been superseded because it used an older source inventory. It is kept as history, not as a current result.

What would change the answer

Better terrain, real hydraulic forcing, validation against an actual flood event, and shelter capacity checked with whoever runs the shelters. Until then the release is labelled a demonstration: not a forecast, not a warning and not an evacuation recommendation.

This is the same rule as the railway floodplain work and the Bangkok world-model post. Say what the dispatcher, or the district office, can actually use. If you cannot measure it, leave the cell empty and say why.
entry.summary: BKK/FLOW puts the PFLOW contract on Bangkok using open data. Its city-scale flood depth is empty on purpose, and the reason is one terrain tile.

entry.title: Looking at 233 million waypoints
entry.content:
Pseudo-PFLOW produces trucks and taxis. The output I work with is about 4.43 million trips and 233 million waypoints. A CSV is not a way to look at that. A notebook map of a random sample is a way to fool yourself, because the sample is always the part that looks fine.

So I built trajectory-viz: a map you can ask questions of. The code is on GitHub under MIT. It is an alpha, and it says so.

What I needed to ask

A calibration table tells you the totals match. It does not tell you whether a truck’s day looks like a truck’s day. For that I wanted:

  • trips filtered by hour, distance, average speed, dwell time and detour ratio;
  • trip chains: how many stops, whether the vehicle comes back, whether it passes through a given box;
  • one vehicle’s whole day, segment by segment, with its speed and its stops;
  • the same view for two fleets side by side.

None of that is exotic. All of it is slow if every question means another script.

The stack, briefly

DuckDB holds trips and waypoints, about 8 GB at PFLOW scale, with 12 indexes on the columns people filter by. FastAPI serves about 30 endpoints on top of it. React, deck.gl and MapLibre draw the map. In Docker it is one container on one port.

The one design decision I would defend is the source registry. A new dataset is a block in sources.yaml, not new backend code. The front end asks the API which vehicle types exist and draws a button for each. That is how a viewer built for two hard-coded fleets now reads GPX tracks, GeoJSON, NDJSON pings, Parquet and ABM trip CSVs. Sources that are only timestamped points get trips cut out of them at ingest.

The bug that never crashes

Taxi IDs restart from 1 in every city. Tokyo taxi #47 and Osaka taxi #47 are different cars with the same integer. Group by vehicle_id and you silently merge two fleets. Every count is plausible. Every chart is wrong.

The fix is boring: a globally unique vehicle_key (taxi:tokyo:47) built at ingest, and a rule that every grouping, distinct count and waypoint join uses it. The same mistake turned up again in a trip-chain query that joined on the old pair of columns. Nothing errored. The fix was checked against a ground-truth join on the Kichijōji database.

Kichijōji

The latest work came from a small question about a pedestrian superblock around Kichijōji. Answering it needed three things the tool did not have. Transport mode had to become a real filter instead of a separate source per mode. Footfall needed its own layer. And there had to be a way to say “pedestrianise this box” and see the trips and vehicle-kilometres that disappear. That last one is a query-time scenario, so no data is rewritten.

The buildings were wrong too. The synthetic footprints around the station came from dissolved city blocks, and the height rule made the biggest blocks the tallest, so the shopping streets turned into 60 m slabs. They are now real PLATEAU footprints with measured heights, 27,029 of them. A map that looks wrong gets ignored, even when the trips on it are right.

What it is not

A dashboard is where you notice something is off. Published margins are where you show it is right. trajectory-viz is the first of those, not the second. The Pseudo-PFLOW numbers that matter stay tied to source statistics, and anything unpublished stays off this blog.

If you have trajectories of your own, the repository ships a synthetic demo day around Kichijōji. pip install -e . and trajectory-viz-demo --serve gets you a map.
entry.summary: A synthetic population needs a map you can question. trajectory-viz, DuckDB under FastAPI, and the vehicle_key bug that never crashes.

entry.title: Tokyo: one city, one action, one output

link.title: Tokyo: one city, one action, one output

entry.content:
Bangkok is a sparse-data, monsoon, fractured-GTFS problem. Tokyo is not. Copying the Bangkok MVP onto a 23-ku basemap would waste the one thing this city has: a population layer and a rail graph that already work.

Same rule as the world-models note: one city + one action type + one daily output.

The unit

  • City: Tokyo metropolitan rail + the surface streets that feed it (JR East, metro, private railways). Freight on the same geography via Pseudo-PFLOW.
  • Actions: a line or corridor closure (typhoon / incident / planned engineering) and its cousin, a pricing or access change (congestion charge trial, express-stop skip). Not a concert. Tokyo already handles concerts.
  • Output: delay and crowding on the parallel corridors, 1–6 hours out, passenger and business-vehicle. A duty officer at a JR control centre already sees the closed line. They do not see a coherent “what the trucks do instead.”

If the screen only restates the delay already on Yahoo Transit, it is not a world model. It is a scraper.

Why Tokyo is not Bangkok with better GTFS

  1. The graph is real and dense. Vertical integration on JR, private railways that own the station, metro as a separate clock — still one of the most complete urban rail objects on Earth. Grounding is not the bottleneck. JR: past, present, future is the institutional layer; the world model is the dynamics layer.
  2. A synthetic population already exists in this lab. Pseudo-PFLOW: on the order of 4.5 million daily business-vehicle trips, 1.5 million-plus truck and taxi agents, 106 zones, calibrated against source statistics. That is the freight that household surveys miss. The world-model job is to roll those agents under an action, not to invent them again.
  3. Operators are not waiting for a startup dashboard. JR East, TMG, and the expressway companies have measurement. Google Mobility AI and DeepETT-class ETA stacks will be judged here on operational metrics. A Tokyo product that only forecasts the next 15 minutes of traffic has already lost.
  4. The rare event is a network event. Typhoon, earthquake inspection, last-train failure, a Shinkansen feeder shock. The photoreal AV world models (Waymo, Cosmos, SceneDiffuser++) will give you the flooded intersection in 4K. They will not tell you whether the Saikyō Line dump lands on the Yamanote or on the Metropolitan Expressway — or on the trucks Pseudo-PFLOW is supposed to be counting.

Data stack (what this lab can actually touch)

Layer Start here Do not pretend
Business vehicles Pseudo-PFLOW agents + published margins Unpublished fit numbers on this blog
Passenger Public counts, congestion reports, GTFS-like feeds where they exist A fused JR+metro+private AFC dump
Network DRM / OSM / published railway GIS A full nationwide digital twin
Action Official closure tweets, planned engineering bulletins, typhoon track A hydrology model of the Sumida
Grounding The real rail graph; Street View only as context tokens Training Genie on Shinjuku

The honest MVP is Pseudo-PFLOW (or a thinner passenger assignment) + a published corridor graph + a one-hot action (this line closed) → delay/crowding on named parallels. A learned residual world model on top, trained on historical closures and typhoon days that are public, not on lab-only traces.

GUFM stays off this page. If a decoder-only trajectory model later becomes the passenger prior, that is a paper, not a product sentence.

What to fake first vs what to learn

Fake first. Close the Chuo Line; dump demand onto the parallel metro and the next JR corridor with a capacity constraint. Show trucks rerouting on the 106-zone system instead of teleporting. This is assignment plus a closure flag. Operators will forgive crude physics. They will not forgive a missing parallel.

Learn next. (s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, c_t)) where (a_t) is the closure/pricing vector and (c_t) is weather and clock. The loss that matters is crowding and delay on the unclosed links, and truck-hours on the zone graph — against DeepETT-class ETAs, not FID.

Do not learn. Photoreal rain at Shibuya scramble. Tokyo does not have a pixel problem.

The Tokyo-shaped hole

Bangkok’s hole is data and SE Asian traffic physics. Tokyo’s hole is action-conditioned coherence on a network that is already observed:

  • Ego vs city → still corridor, but the corridor is a JR line plus the expressway the trucks take.
  • Grounding → already have the graph; do not invent it.
  • Sparse-data → not the constraint inside the 23 wards; it is the constraint the moment you care about nationwide freight (that is why Pseudo-PFLOW is nationwide, 106 zones, not one ward).
  • Behavior not pixels → activity sequences for passengers if you have them; business-vehicle diaries from the ABM if you do not.
  • Closed-loop with operators → they already have a dashboard. The paint-an-action tool has to beat “the control centre already knows.” The wedge is freight + parallel crowding jointly, which those dashboards split across agencies.

Do not merge the two cities

A single “Asian mega-city world model” will average away the only useful facts: Bangkok needs synthetic people and monsoon as an action; Tokyo needs synthetic freight and a line closure as an action. Same math, (s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, c_t)). Different (a), different data, different buyer.

If I only ship one web MVP, Bangkok is the one Google will underserve. If I only ship one lab demo from CSIS, Tokyo is the one where Pseudo-PFLOW can be the prior tomorrow morning.
entry.summary: Dense rails, a synthetic freight population, operators who already have dashboards. The world-model product here is what happens to the corridor after you close a line — not whether you can forecast the next train.

entry.title: Bangkok: one city, one action, one output

link.title: Bangkok: one city, one action, one output

entry.content:
The world-models note ended on a rule: pick one city + one action type + one output people would open daily. This is Bangkok. Tokyo is a separate post. They are not the same product with a different basemap.

The unit

  • City: Bangkok (BMA + the rail spines that actually move people: BTS, MRT, ARL, BMTA, boats).
  • Actions: flood / royal motorcade / concert (plus the ordinary cousin: a feeder cut or a station closure).
  • Output: BTS + bus crowding, three hours ahead, by line and by station group — not a citywide delay index.

If that screen is not something a duty officer at BMTA or a BTS station master would keep open, it is a paper. The consumer view is thinner: “will my bus be wrecked at 18:00.”

Why Bangkok is not a METR-LA fine-tune

Almost every photorealistic world model in 2026 sits in a car on a well-mapped street graph. Bangkok’s binding constraints are the opposite:

  1. Sparse, fractured open data. GTFS is incomplete or stale depending on the operator. BMTA, BTS, MRT, and boats do not share a clock. TODM exists because finding the table is still a week of work. A world model that assumes Uber-scale probe density will silently train on the CBD and call it the city.
  2. Physics Waymo will not cover. Motorcycle filtering, songthaew stop patterns, jaywalk regimes, sidewalks that are not sidewalks. That is the infrastructure-centric world-model argument in miniature: a roadside camera at a few intersections has years of those behaviors. Fleet AV data does not.
  3. Monsoon as an action, not weather noise. We already treated water on the railway as an operating rule (FRI in centimetres) in the flood orals. The missing piece is the urban graph: when a canal road goes under, which BTS stations overload, which bus routes die, who is stuck in a songthaew that never comes.
  4. Land use is local. The Blue Line GWR is the warning: a citywide elasticity will mis-state both Siam and Tha Phra. An intervention rollout that uses one demand head for the whole BMA will do the same.

Google Mobility AI will underserve this city relative to Tokyo. That is the product reason to be here.

Data stack (what you can actually start from)

Do not wait for a 70,000-household survey refresh.

Layer Start here Do not pretend
Synthetic population / traces WorldMove (Bangkok is in the 1,600-city set) That WorldMove is the HTS
Open catalogues TODM + MOT / BMA portals That BMTA GTFS is complete
Network OSM + whatever official rail station lists exist A fused multi-operator GTFS
Grounding Street View / map tiles as layout condition, not as a video world Genie-invented soi geometry
Weather / flood Public rainfall + the railway FRI work as a prior on how water becomes an operating rule A hydrology digital twin on day one
Behavior HTS 2022 margins where they exist; mode shares as calibration targets Microdata on GitHub

The honest MVP is WorldMove + OSM + a handful of counted corridors + rainfall, with a learned residual on top of a calibrated simulator. Not Atlas.

What to fake first vs what to learn

Fake (simulator) first. Lane closure, station closure, concert centroid: a macroscopic or mesoscopic assignment (even a four-step with a time-of-day slice, which is how I was trained in Nakhon Ratchasima) plus crude crowding = volume / capacity on BTS links. Operators already think in that language.

Learn next. The residual world model: given state (flows, weather, clock, a one-hot action) predict the distribution of crowding three hours out, including the tail. Flood and motorcade are rare; that is why you need a world model instead of last-week’s LSTM. You will not have enough labelled motorcades. You will have enough ordinary evenings to learn the base dynamics, then condition on the rare action with a lot of humility and a simulator prior.

Do not learn. Photoreal rain on Sukhumvit. Useless if the mode split is wrong.

The Bangkok-shaped hole

The world-models post listed five breaks. Bangkok hits all of them except “we have no city”:

  • Ego vs city → corridor crowding, not a camera in a taxi.
  • Grounding → real BTS/MRT graph, not a generated street.
  • Sparse-data → WorldMove + TODM, not METR-LA.
  • Behavior not pixels → MobilityGen-style activity sequences if you can; HTS margins if you cannot.
  • Closed-loop with operators → a web paint-an-action tool, Thai-language, three-hour horizon.

Tokyo, next, has the opposite problem: the synthetic population and the sensors already exist. The missing object is still the action.
entry.summary: Sparse data, monsoon physics, a fractured transit graph. The world-model product here is not a robotaxi clip — it is crowding three hours after a flood, a concert, or a motorcade.

entry.title: World models are the next layer for mobility

link.title: World models are the next layer for mobility

entry.content:
World models are the right next layer for mobility work. They do not just forecast the next 15 minutes of traffic. They learn how the city evolves under actions, so you can roll out “what if” futures. That is the gap between a dashboard and infrastructure people would actually use.

This sits next to Pseudo-PFLOW: a synthetic population when surveys miss the vehicles, and a world model when you need those agents to stay coherent after you close a lane. It is not a GUFM paper. It is why action-conditioned dynamics belong in the same lab as generative mobility.

What a world model is (in 2026)

Classic mobility models answer: given history, what happens next?

A world model answers: given the current state of the world + an action, how does the world evolve? You compress observations (GPS, cameras, cell load, maps, weather) into a latent state, then roll that state forward under hypothetical interventions.

Three capabilities matter for transportation:

Capability Mobility version
Predict Next location, flow, travel time, occupancy
Simulate Counterfactual: close a lane, retune a signal, add BRT, a concert, flooding
Control / plan Choose actions whose imagined futures look good (delay, emissions, safety)

That last piece is why operators care. Static forecast models break the moment you change the network. World models are built to stay coherent under action trajectories.

Three stacks that actually predict mobility

1. Street-level / AV world models (highest fidelity)

These generate the next seconds–minutes of a driving scene: other vehicles, pedestrians, signals, weather, even lidar.

  • Waymo World Model (Feb 2026) is Genie 3 specialized for driving. Controllable via driving actions, scene layout (roads, signals, other users), and language (weather, time of day). Used to rehearse rare events that never show up in fleet data.
  • Genie 3 + Street View (May 2026) grounds those worlds in real streets, not invented cities. That is the geoAI hook: simulation anchored to an actual place.
  • NVIDIA Cosmos / OmniDreams: open(ish) world foundation models for physical AI. Cosmos 3 unifies generation + reasoning + action. OmniDreams does real-time closed-loop AV simulation — the policy drives, the world model renders the next sensor frame. Cosmos 3 is also being used for traffic-anomaly reasoning on city cameras.
  • AutoWorld (Mar 2026): self-supervised world model from raw LiDAR occupancy → multi-agent traffic simulation (Waymo Sim Agents). Better in partially observed scenes than trajectory-only baselines.
  • SceneDiffuser++: one generative world model that does city-scale A-to-B simulation — spawn/despawn agents, traffic lights, occlusion, long rollouts on a map.
  • Infrastructure-centric world models (I-WM) (2026 vision paper): almost everything above is ego-vehicle. Roadside cameras/lidar have the opposite strength — years of behavior at one intersection, including rare crashes. Proposal: combine roadside temporal depth with vehicle spatial breadth, then share latents over V2X. This is the most underrated angle for public infra.

If you only care about robotaxis, stop here. If you care about cities, keep going.

2. Network / population mobility world models (the planning layer)

This is closer to “will people actually use this transit change?”

  • MobiWM (Apr 2026, Tsinghua-adjacent group around Yong Li): first explicit world model for mobile networks. State = cell traffic; actions = antenna power / azimuth / tilt. Multimodal context (images + sequences) with shared spatial semantics. Unlimited-horizon rollout for counterfactual planning across 31,900 cells / 9 districts; at least 16.4% better distributional fidelity than forecast baselines on average; used as a learned surrogate inside actor-critic optimization.
  • MobiWorld: generative foundation model that emits both element-level data (traffic, user distribution, app usage, mobility trajectories) and system KPIs (throughput, coverage, energy) under policies and urban context. Same group’s framing of “what a world model even is for networks.”
  • DeepMobility (PNAS Nexus, 2025): generative model that jointly captures individual trajectories and city-wide flows, and actually reproduces known scaling laws of human mobility instead of memorizing training traces. Trained only on locations; transferred across Chinese megacities and Senegal. Direct use: synthetic mobility for planning, epidemics, traffic engineering.
  • MobilityGen (2025–26): diffusion model of multi-day activity-travel sequences (purpose, mode, destination) coupled to the built environment. Enables analyses static OD matrices cannot: mode-specific access to urban space, co-presence / segregation.
  • WorldMove (Scientific Data, 2026): open synthetic human-mobility data for 1,600+ cities. Used with a microscopic simulator (MOSS) for traffic and emissions; mixing synthetic + sparse real traces improves forecasting when real data is thin (Shanghai, Nanchang, New York). This is the data layer a Bangkok-scale side project can actually start from. Pipeline: tsinghua-fib-lab/WorldMove.
  • AgentMove: LLM agent for zero-shot next-location prediction using spatial-temporal memory + a “world knowledge generator” over addresses. Works across 12 cities without per-user training data — important where privacy / data access is the blocker.
  • Google Mobility AI (2025, updated Jan 2026): measurement → digital-twin simulation (Traffic Simulation API) → optimization (signals, routing, evacuations, congestion pricing eval). Geospatial foundation embeddings + generative geospatial reasoning. Aimed at agencies, not consumers.
  • Uber’s DeepETT (2026) is not a world model, but shows the production bar: graph-aware transformer on a ~100M-segment global road graph, 6% better long-trip ETAs, claimed ~$100M annual value. World models will be judged against systems like this on operational metrics, not FID.

3. General spatial world models (the platform layer)

  • World Labs (Fei-Fei Li): Marble (generate/explore 3D worlds from text/image/video, World API Jan 2026) → RTFM (real-time interactive frames with spatial memory) → Atlas (1 Sept 2026): omni model over text/image/video/3D, reconstruction + space-time simulation, Real-to-Sim for robotics. Their claim is that spatial intelligence is the next stack after language.
  • Seoul World Model: grounds video world models in a real metropolis via street-view retrieval. Most generic world models drift off the actual street graph; this one is built to stay on it.

For a mobility product, you usually do not train Atlas/Genie from scratch. You use them as a grounded simulator or as a prior, then attach a cheaper mobility head (flows, ETAs, demand).

Why this is different from “just another traffic LSTM”

Old stack World-model stack
Predict (x_{t+1}) from (x_{\le t}) Predict (s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, c_t))
Breaks when you change signals, lanes, fares Rollout is defined under those actions
One most-likely future Multimodal futures (brake vs go, rain vs dry)
City-specific trained graph Foundation + city conditioning / few-shot
Needs dense sensors Can mix sparse GPS + synthetic WorldMove + street view

The papers that matter most for this thesis (mobility behavior + geoAI + usable infra) are the ones that treat actions and context as first-class: MobiWM, I-WM, MobilityGen, SceneDiffuser++, Google Mobility AI. Everything else is either AV-only or a better forecaster.

What is still broken (and therefore buildable)

  1. Ego vs city. Almost all photorealistic world models sit in a car. Cities need intersection- and network-level models that answer “what happens to the corridor,” not “what does my camera see.” I-WM is a research vision, not a product.
  2. Grounding. Generative worlds invent geometry. Mobility infra cannot. Street View + Genie, Seoul WM, and map-conditioned SceneDiffuser++ are the pattern: retrieve or condition on real layout.
  3. Sparse-data cities. WorldMove + AgentMove + city-conditioned memory exist because most of the world is not METR-LA. Bangkok, secondary Thai cities, and most ASEAN metros live here.
  4. Behavior, not pixels. Predicting photoreal rain is useless if mode choice and activity sequences are wrong. DeepMobility / MobilityGen are the behavioral world models; they are under-productized.
  5. Closed-loop with operators. Google has a Traffic Simulation API for agencies. There is no good open, intervention-first web tool: “draw a lane closure / new stop / fare change → see demand, delay, and who is harmed.” That is a product-shaped hole.

Side-project shapes that people would actually use

Given the focus here (webs + infra for transportation behavior, geoAI):

A. Intervention sandbox (highest product fit)
Map of a real city → user paints an action (roadwork, flood, concert, new BTS feeder, signal retiming) → world-model rollout of flows / ETAs / crowding for 1–24h. Backend can start crude (calibrated simulator + learned residual world model) and get smarter. Agencies and event operators pay for this; commuters use a thin consumer view (“will my bus be wrecked at 18:00”).

B. Sparse-city mobility twin
WorldMove-style synthetic population + whatever open GPS/transit GTFS you can get + street-view grounding. Target a city that Google Mobility AI will underserve. Evaluate on next-location, OD, and travel-time under interventions, not just next-step RMSE.

C. Roadside / intersection world model
Fixed camera or cheap lidar at a few Bangkok intersections. Learn long-horizon behavioral distributions (jaywalk regimes, motorcycle filtering, songthaew stop patterns). This is I-WM in miniature and is unique to SE Asia traffic physics that Waymo/NVIDIA data will not cover.

D. Mobility head on a spatial foundation
Don’t train a Genie. Use embeddings / reconstructed 3D / Street View as context tokens, then train a small action-conditioned predictor for demand and travel time. Invert the usual “mobility graph improves urban embeddings” story: use the foundation to improve mobility.

Suggested reading order (dense, 2025–26)

  1. Survey: A Survey of World Models for Autonomous Driving — taxonomy of generation vs planning.
  2. MobiWM + MobiWorld — best “world model for mobility systems” papers, not cars.
  3. DeepMobility + MobilityGen + WorldMove — human behavior layer + open data.
  4. Waymo WM + Genie/Street View + SceneDiffuser++ — what frontier simulation looks like.
  5. Infrastructure-centric WM — the public-infra research agenda.
  6. Google Mobility AI + Uber DeepETT — what production systems already ship without calling themselves world models.

One city + one action + one daily output, written out: Bangkok (flood / motorcade / concert → BTS+bus crowding, three hours) and Tokyo (line closure → parallel crowding and trucks). Same (s_{t+1}=f(s_t,a_t,c_t)). Different (a), different data, different buyer.

Sources I actually opened

  • Qi, Chai, Wang, Li. MobiWM, arXiv:2604.08199, 2026. (≥16.4% average gain vs baselines; 31,900 cells / 9 districts.)
  • Chai, Yuan, Li. MobiWorld, arXiv:2507.09462, 2025.
  • Yuan, Ding, Jin, Li. DeepMobility, PNAS Nexus 4(5), pgaf081, 2025.
  • Yuan, Zhang, Ding, Li. WorldMove, Scientific Data, 2026. Data: worldmove.
entry.summary: Not the next 15 minutes of traffic — how the city evolves under actions. Predict, simulate, plan. What 2025–26 actually built, and the product-shaped hole that is left.

entry.title: Pseudo-PFLOW: making the freight that surveys miss

link.title: Pseudo-PFLOW: making the freight that surveys miss

entry.content:
Status: in progress, CSIS / Sekimoto Lab, The University of Tokyo. Project card: Pseudo-PFLOW. This post is the question and the setup. It is not a results paper.

Why it exists

Household travel surveys are where I learned the craft. They are also almost silent on business vehicles. Trucks and taxis eat urban road space and they barely appear in a diary of “where did you go yesterday.” If you only calibrate a city on households, you are modelling the commute and calling it traffic.

Pseudo-PFLOW is a nationwide agent-based picture of those missing vehicles: synthetic trucks and taxis, daily activity, assigned to a zone system, checked against statistics that are published. The CV numbers I will repeat, and not add to:

  • on the order of 4.5 million daily trips
  • 1.5 million-plus truck and taxi agents
  • 106 zones
  • calibration and cross-verification against source statistics (not against a private GPS dump I will not name here)

I also wrote technical documentation for the truck and taxi ABMs: calibration, data provenance, cross-verification. That sentence is on the CV because provenance is the method. If you cannot say which table an agent’s trip rate came from, you have a simulator, not a synthetic population.

What the model is for

A planner who wants national freight and taxi load on the network without waiting for a new establishment survey. A researcher who wants a baseline of business-vehicle kilometres that a passenger-only four-step will not give them. Later, a check on whether a generative mobility model is inventing truck-shaped trips or only commuting.

It is not a digital twin of every depot. It is not GUFM. GUFM is the other Tokyo thread and it is not this series.

How I am willing to talk about progress

Same rules as the method post:

  • The unit is the agent-day, the geography is the zone, the judge is a published margin (counts, totals, shares) — not a loss curve.
  • If a calibration gap is not in a public figure, it is not on this blog.
  • Code and papers, when they exist as citable objects, go on publications and GitHub. Until then, the project page is the placeholder.

When there is a paper, this post gets a DOI line. Until then: 4.5 million trips, 106 zones, and a refusal to fake the fit.

The layer after a synthetic population is action-conditioned dynamics: world models for mobility.
entry.summary: In progress at CSIS — a nationwide ABM of trucks and taxis, 4.5 million daily trips, 106 zones. Method and question only; no unpublished fit.

entry.title: An accessibility index for Bangkok
entry.content:
Paper: Wanichjaroenporn, Wongkaew, Muanyoksakul, Surangsrirout, Bunditsakulchai. Public Transport Accessibility Index for Bangkok and Its Application. Transportation Research Record, accepted (2025). Listings: publications, research one-pager.

This is Kongtup’s lead. I am writing as a coauthor, not as the PI. I will not paste a results table the journal has not put on a DOI yet.

Question

Bangkok talks about “coverage” as if a station on the map were access. Coverage is geometry. Accessibility is whether a person at a given place, at a given time, can reach the places that count, at a cost of time (and usually money) they will actually pay. The paper builds an index for that, then an application — without the application the index is a colour ramp.

The user is a planner who needs to see where public transport fails, not a ranking of cities for a press release.

What I am willing to say before the DOI

  • The object is a public-transport accessibility index for Bangkok, plus a use of that index (spatial inequality in access — that is the application named in the abstract we list).
  • I treat a single citywide accessibility number as a headline, not a finding. The finding is the map and the comparison (who is in the high tail, who is in the low tail, what happens if access to the station changes mode).
  • This sits next to the Blue Line GWR. GWR asks how land use loads a station. The index asks whether you can use the system at all. They are not substitutes.

Coauthorship, plainly

Wanichjaroenporn first. Bunditsakulchai last. I am in the middle with Wachira and Nattakarn. If you cite it, cite the author order. If you only need the ridership–land-use paper, that is the other one, and I am first author there.

What comes after the DOI

When TRR assigns a link, it goes on papers.bib and this post gets a one-line update. Until then the honest status is accepted, which is already better than “we have an index.” I will not fill the gap with numbers from a related thesis or a workshop slide.

If you want the live academic record while that happens: wattwong103.github.io/research.
entry.summary: Transportation Research Record (accepted): Kongtup Wanichjaroenporn led; I am a coauthor. What the index is for, and what I will not pretend it is.
